h1: Budget lines for a craft whisky distillery
title: Budget Lines for a Craft Distillery | Craft Beer School
desc: The capital and running cost lines a craft whisky distillery in India must plan for, plus the ones founders most often leave out.
teaser: Stills get the attention. The budget lines that sink craft distilleries are casks, utilities and three years of waiting.
standfirst: Most first budgets for a craft whisky distillery get the stills roughly right and miss half of everything else. Here are the lines a realistic budget needs, grouped the way a lender or investor will want to see them. Every figure in it should come from current quotes, not from memory.
sections: Start with the shape, not the numbers

A whisky distillery's budget has three blocks: the capital to build it, the running costs to operate it and the working capital to carry stock until it can be sold. The third block is the one that surprises people. Scotch needs at least three years in oak before it can be called whisky. Even where local rules allow a younger release, quality whisky usually takes years. Every litre you make in year one is cash on a rack, not cash in the bank.

We would not put a single rupee figure in a guide like this, because prices move and every site differs. What we can give is the list of lines. A budget missing any of them is incomplete.

• Land and building. Purchase or lease, civil works, drainage, fire separation and a warehouse sized for several years of production.
  • Grain handling. Intake, storage, cleaning and a mill, with dust control.
  • Brewhouse side. Mash tun, hot water tank, wort cooling and washbacks.
  • Stills. Wash still, spirit still, condensers, spirit safe, receivers and spirit store.
  • Utilities. Steam boiler, cooling water system, compressed air, electrical supply and backup power.
  • Effluent treatment. Pot ale and spent lees handling, often a large and underestimated line in India.
  • Filling and warehousing. Filling station, racking or palletised storage and handling equipment.
  • Laboratory. Hydrometers or a density meter, temperature correction, basic QC kit.
  • Bottling. Either an in-house line or the cost of a contract bottler.

Operating costs fall into familiar groups: grain, yeast, enzymes if you use them, energy, water, effluent treatment, labour, maintenance, insurance and compliance. Two deserve a warning.

Energy is larger than many founders expect. Mashing needs hot water at around 63 to 65 °C. Distillation boils large volumes of wash. Steam generation is a big share of running cost, so your fuel choice matters.

Compliance is a running cost too. Excise staff time, licence renewals, label registrations and the record keeping the state excise department requires all need people and money every year.
Casks are a capital line and a running cost

Casks deserve their own section. Every litre of new make needs a cask. Casks are bought before the whisky is sold. A 200 litre ex-bourbon barrel filled at 63.5% ABV holds 127 litres of pure alcohol. If you make 50,000 litres of pure alcohol a year, you need nearly 400 barrels a year at that size, before any losses. Larger casks change the count. Imported casks carry freight and import costs. The supply is not guaranteed. Our guide to sourcing oak casks for an Indian distillery goes into the options.

Plan casks for every production year until the first release, not just year one.
Working capital is the big one

Here is the arithmetic that matters. Suppose you plan a first release at four years. That means four years of grain, energy, labour, casks and warehouse costs sitting in stock before any whisky revenue arrives. Add the loss to evaporation, which in Indian heat runs well above the roughly 2% a year often quoted for Scotland. You pay to make a litre, then lose part of it while you wait.

This is why many craft distilleries sell gin or other unaged spirits early. It is also why some sell cask shares. Both fund the wait. Neither removes it. Lenders will ask how you fund years of stock before you sell whisky. Your budget should answer before they ask.

• Licensing and consultancy fees before construction starts, which vary by state.
  • Commissioning runs and the spirit that does not meet spec in early batches.
  • Spare parts, particularly for pumps, seals and steam fittings.
  • Training for operators who have never run a still.
  • Brand, label design and label registration in each state you plan to sell in.
  • Contingency, which experienced builders set well above ten percent for a first project.

A lender or investor reads a distillery budget looking for three things. First, whether the capital lines are complete and based on quotes. Second, whether the running costs match the output, which they will test by dividing total running cost by litres of pure alcohol produced. Third, whether the working capital is funded until whisky revenue starts.

Make that test easy for them. Show yearly output in litres of pure alcohol, the cost per litre of pure alcohol at each stage and the stock held at each year end. If your plan assumes 50,000 litres of pure alcohol a year and four years to first release, show the four years of stock clearly with its losses. A plan that hides the stock build in a single line looks naive. One that shows it plainly looks like a team that understands whisky.

Open a spreadsheet with three tabs: capital, running costs and working capital to first release. Put every line above into the right tab, even if the cell stays empty for now. Then mark which numbers come from real quotes and which are guesses. Understanding the process well enough to cost each stage is where most founders find they need help.
faqs: What is the biggest cost for a new whisky distillery?
Stills and buildings are visible, but the working capital to carry several years of maturing stock before the first whisky sale is often the largest commitment.
How many casks does a craft distillery need?
Divide yearly pure alcohol output by the pure alcohol per cask. A 200 litre barrel at 63.5% ABV holds 127 litres of pure alcohol.
Why do distilleries sell gin while whisky ages?
Unaged spirits can be sold within weeks, which brings in revenue and builds a brand while the whisky matures.
